idiom_name: String.Intern / IsInterned and NameTable atomization; ConcurrentDictionary pool for custom keys
implementation_notes: The CLR provides the factory role for strings: String.Intern returns the canonical reference from the runtime intern pool and IsInterned returns null when the value has never been interned, while the XML stack documents atomization directly - NameTable.Add/Get stores each element or attribute name once so later comparisons can be ReferenceEquals instead of string comparison. For your own intrinsic types the pool is a ConcurrentDictionary keyed by the intrinsic state (or a ConditionalWeakTable when entries must die with their keys), the flyweight stays an immutable class with readonly fields, and the extrinsic state belongs in a separate per-entity object. Note what interning does not do: it shares whole values, so the intrinsic/extrinsic split of your own object is still your design decision.
pitfalls: The intern pool is process-wide and its entries are not released until the CLR terminates, so interning dynamic, attacker-controlled or secret-bearing strings is a memory leak and a disclosure risk; use your own weak or bounded pool.
Literal interning is not guaranteed - the compiler emits NoStringInterning by default and native AOT keeps it off - so ReferenceEquals on literals is an optimization, never a correctness contract.
A static ConcurrentDictionary pool never shrinks: with unbounded keys it leaks. Prefer ConditionalWeakTable, a bounded cache with eviction, or explicit removal.

readonly fields block reassignment but not mutation of the referenced object: a mutable List or array inside a shared flyweight is still writable by every context. Expose IReadOnlyList or ImmutableArray.
